1.0.s.en: (1) Paul's greeting and his defense of his apostleship

1.0.0.en: Not of men, neither by man: that is, he was not a disciple at the hands of any human being, and no man sent him to preach. But by Jesus Christ, and God the Father: as one single source of the mission, for the Father and the Son are one in essence. This is a confession of the divinity of Christ, since St. Paul affirms that He (Christ) is not of men, that is, He is not an ordinary man.

1.0.1.en: Who raised him from the dead: the resurrection of Christ from the dead is ascribed sometimes to the Father and sometimes to Christ Himself. If St. Paul ascribed it to the Father here, we must not forget that Christ said of His death and resurrection, "I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (Jn 10:18). St. Paul begins his epistle in a severe tone, unlike his custom, by identifying himself and his apostleship, which is from the Lord Christ Himself, like all the apostles and disciples whom Christ sent during His incarnation. He declares that he was not sent by the apostles or by any human source, in order to answer those who cast doubt on his apostleship on the pretext that he had not seen Christ on earth and was therefore lesser in standing and in the worth of what he teaches. They did this in order to spread their strange teachings about the necessity of circumcision, of becoming Jews, and of submitting to the works of the Law.

1.1.0.en: The churches of Galatia: Galatia was a province or region that included several churches. It was not one city or one church, but several churches scattered in some cities such as "Ancyra" and "Thafium", and the strange teachings had spread throughout the whole region. He sends them greetings in his own name and in the name of those who were with him in the ministry at that time.

1.2.0.en: Grace be to you and peace: he wishes them the work of God's grace within them, and especially the peace that fills their hearts.

1.2.1.en: Our Father: that is, through redemption we received the grace of adoption.

1.2.2.en: That he might deliver us from this present evil world: we are no longer enslaved to sin.

1.2.3.en: The Apostle Paul shows the oneness of the Father and the Son in essence as the source of grace and peace. Although the Son offered the redemption, it was accomplished according to the will of the Father. Thus he shows the oneness of will between the Father and the Son, and shows by this that salvation is by the blood of Christ, and not by the works of the Law as the false teachers proclaim.

1.3.0.en: The Apostle concludes the introduction by offering glory to God, for He is worthy of glory and honor forever..

1.3.1.en: Do we always give glory and thanks to God for the grace of redemption and adoption, and because He keeps us every day from the evils of this present world so that we may be with Him in eternity?!

1.4.s.en: (2) Rejecting false teachings and anathema on those who follow them

1.4.0.en: So soon: the Galatians believed and were baptized six years before the writing of this epistle, when Paul visited them on his first journey, and likewise on his second journey, three years ago, they were holding fast to the sound faith. So their change took place a short time before the writing of this epistle, and the Apostle marvels that they were influenced by the teaching of the false teachers and left the faith in which they had lived for about five years.

1.4.1.en: Another gospel: another, different message, that is, the teachings of the false teachers.

1.4.2.en: In his epistles, after the introduction, St. Paul was accustomed to give thanks to God for those to whom he was writing. Here, however, he begins with a sharp rebuke because of the gravity of turning away from the right faith, for it is a matter of life or death. Yet he gives them hope of repentance: he does not say, "You have been removed, and it is finished," but "you are removed," that is, they can still repent, return, and stand firm in the faith. He expresses astonishment at the swiftness of their turning, when they had believed at his hands by the call of God, who called them to the grace of Christ to receive redemption and free salvation, to another call, to salvation by the works of the Law and circumcision.

1.5.0.en: Which is not another: that is, it is not a gospel at all, and those who proclaim it trouble you, for there is only one Gospel. Even if the four Evangelists wrote it, its meaning and its message are one, whereas a single man may write a book that contradicts itself.

1.6.0.en: If we preach: here Paul places himself in the rank of the apostles, and says that his message is the very same Gospel as that of the rest of the apostles. The false teachers claimed that after Paul had preached to Galatia he changed his teaching. So here he pronounces anathema on himself if he had changed his preaching as the false teachers accuse him, in order to confirm the true message about Christ which he preached to them.

1.6.1.en: An angel from heaven: Satan, who can change his form into the likeness of an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14). Than that which we have preached: that is, what you received.

1.6.3.en: Here Paul uses the authority of binding and loosing, as the Lord delivered it to His disciples. For this reason St. Paul stressed faithfulness in handing down the faith (2 Tim 1:13), (1 Cor 11:23), (2 Tim 2:2). The Coptic Orthodox Church has offered thousands of martyrs to preserve what she received of the sound faith, so we must hold fast to the faith that we received from the Fathers. We note that apostolic authority was not for boasting but for edification (2 Cor 10:8). And Paul places himself within the circle of anathema if he should change his faith. By this he makes clear that he does not despise the message of the rest of the apostles, but that the Christian message has one source, which is the Holy Spirit.

1.7.0.en: Paul used to please men in all things, even at his own expense: "Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking mine own profit" (1 Cor 10:33). But when the matter concerns faith and doctrine, he does not yield and shows no readiness for leniency, for he submits to the truth that is in Christ because he is the servant of Christ and not of men.

1.7.1.en: Do we please God or men?..! Pilate was sure of the innocence of Christ, but he pleased the people and handed Him over to them to be crucified. Everyone who pleases men at the expense of God tramples on the right of Christ. Paul endured very many sufferings that he could have avoided had he said what pleases men, but he was careful to preserve the soundness of the faith that is pleasing to Christ.

1.8.s.en: (3) Paul's calling and his life before the faith

1.8.0.en: The Apostle defends the truth of the Gospel that he preaches, and says that he did not receive his teachings from a man but by the revelation of Jesus Christ Himself, and this is sufficient proof of the truth of his message. This must have happened directly from the Lord during the period of his retreat in the Arabian desert near Damascus, after he saw the Lord (v. 17).

1.9.0.en: Beyond measure: that is, without mercy.

1.9.1.en: Wasted it: that is, destroyed it and scattered the believers in it, harming them in every way, even to the point of killing.

1.9.2.en: My equals: that is, those of his own age among the children of Israel.

1.9.3.en: The Apostle Paul reminds them of his former conduct, and how he was a Jew zealous for the teachings of Moses, and advanced in the learning of the Jewish religion because he had studied at the feet of the greatest teacher of the Law, Gamaliel (Acts 22:3, Phil 3:5, 1 Tim 1:13). He does this in order to show the power of divine grace in his life, since he had been a greater persecutor of the Christians than his equals. But when the Lord Jesus called him, he turned with all his energy to building the Church of Christ, after he had been working to destroy it. He had been a Jewish religious leader, fanatical for the Pharisaic traditions of the Law, but after he came to know the truth he turned completely to defending Christianity and preaching it.

1.9.4.en: Be ready to hear the other opinion, and God will guide you, however far you have strayed, and you will return to the truth. Do not neglect the opinion of others or interrupt them, but pray while you listen to them, and you will learn from everyone and grow in wisdom from God day by day.

1.10.s.en: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

1.10.0.en: Separated me from my mother's womb: his calling was from his mother's womb, by the foreknowledge of God who set him apart for a special mission, as He set apart John the Baptist from his mother's womb.

1.10.1.en: That I might preach him among the heathen (the Gentiles): Paul's preaching was focused on the lands of the world filled with the Gentiles, and he did not preach in Judea. But this does not mean that he did not preach to the few Jews living among the Gentiles; rather, he cared for them because they had the prophecies about Christ, and they helped him in his ministry in many countries.

1.10.2.en: Truly a change took place in the life of the Apostle Paul as he was on the way to Damascus, when he was going to persecute the Church of Christ. When God revealed Himself to Paul, he accepted the call, and it pleased God to reveal His Son in him. St. John Chrysostom says that Paul said "to reveal his Son in me" and did not say "to me", in order to show that he did not receive the faith by words alone but by the work of the Holy Spirit in him: "I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). So his life and his conduct were changed.

1.10.3.en: Immediately: Paul accepted the call and went out to the desert (east of the Jordan) and stayed there three years for prayer and retreat, for studying the prophecies about Christ, for reviewing what he had studied, and for seeking God's counsel. In his humility he did not mention this in his epistle, and said:

1.10.4.en: I conferred not with flesh and blood: he is being careful because of those who cast doubt on his apostleship, so he affirms that his calling was from Christ directly and that he sought the counsel of no one, but went straight to his retreat in the desert. St. Paul shows that when God called him on his way to Damascus, he believed and was baptized, and then went out to the Arabian desert near Damascus in retreat for three years, in which he received from Christ all the teachings, so that he became an apostle of His like the rest of the twelve disciples.

1.11.0.en: Them which were apostles before me: the gathering of the apostles and the center of the preaching was in Jerusalem, and Paul did not go to them to consult them. Here he declares that he is an apostle, and that the disciples of Christ were apostles before him.

1.11.1.en: Arabia: a desert near the city of Damascus in Syria, which is different from the Arabian peninsula or the desert of Sinai.

1.11.2.en: Damascus: an ancient city that still has the same name today, as the capital of Syria.

1.11.3.en: Although Paul stayed some days in Damascus after Ananias baptized him, he did not go up to Jerusalem but went out into the wilderness, and returned with a burning, fiery heart after receiving his teachings from the Lord Himself.

1.12.0.en: Three years: counted from his baptism at the hands of Ananias; he spent them in the Arabian desert, then returned to Damascus for a short time and went from there to Jerusalem.

1.12.1.en: When Paul went up to Jerusalem to become acquainted with Peter, he stayed there only 15 days, and met with James, whom he mentions with reverence, saying "the Lord's brother". He was the son of Mary the wife of Clopas and the sister of the Virgin Mary, and was bishop of Jerusalem. He did not meet any of the other apostles, because they were preaching outside Jerusalem. Thus he declares that he was not working alone, but in a spirit not separate from the leadership of the Church. And he was not hasty to meet the Apostle Peter right after his baptism, because the field of his preaching was among the Gentiles and not among the Jews like Peter, as Christ declared to him (Acts 22:17-21).

1.13.0.en: The Apostle Paul went on to serve in Antioch and Cilicia (Tarsus, his homeland) to preach among the Gentiles. He did not go up to Jerusalem to learn from Peter, but to become acquainted with him. And he says the truth, with God as his witness, that he does not lie.

1.14.0.en: St. Paul humbly mentions his former errors, and how the churches of Jewish origin accepted him after his conversion even though they had not seen him before, but had only heard of his past and his cruelty in persecuting the Christians.

1.15.0.en: The believers in the churches of Judea used to pray for him, and God answered their petition, so they glorified God because of His work in Paul's life. His acceptance of God's call had as its result that he said, "God reveals ... in me ... they glorified God in me."

1.15.1.en: The Lord Christ commanded us, "That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Mt 5:16). Are we like that?... If the Church offers glorification to God on the feasts of the saints because Christ lived in them and appeared by His light and teachings in their practical lives, does our life glorify God or cause others to stumble?! And do we pray for our repentance and the repentance of others so that God may be glorified in us?.!

2.0.s.en: (1) Paul presents his message to the council of Jerusalem

2.0.0.en: Fourteen years: this is most probably counted from the time of the calling of the Apostle Paul, and so this is not his first journey to Jerusalem, which was in the year 38 A.D. (Acts 9:26-30). Barnabas: the meaning of his name is son of exhortation (Acts 4:36); he was known for generosity, and he knew Paul and accompanied him on his first journey.

2.0.1.en: Titus: of Greek origin, one of Paul's disciples and companions.

2.0.2.en: Paul went to Jerusalem to present his message to the apostles, because of the false teachers who cast doubt on his apostleship and proclaimed the necessity of circumcision and the works of the Law for those converted from among the Gentiles.

2.1.0.en: Privately: Paul met in secret with the pillars of the Church, who were James the brother of the Lord, bishop of Jerusalem, and Peter and John, and then met with the whole council, which included the rest of the apostles and the priests (Acts 15:6). He met first with the three who were of reputation so that it would be easier to persuade the large council that included the apostles and the priests. All these meetings were held on a limited scale so as not to stir up the Jews in Jerusalem.

2.1.1.en: In vain: Paul does not doubt his preaching, because Christ is the One who taught him it. But by "in vain" he means that his preaching might be wrong in the eyes of the apostles. So he wanted to present what he preaches and obtain their agreement to it, so that the false teachers would not cast doubt on what he teaches.

2.1.2.en: Paul's movements were always by heavenly revelation and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and for this reason we find him at one time saying that the Spirit forbade them. This is the life of the saints, who move by God's guidance and not out of enthusiasm for some idea. And the Holy Spirit gathered in Jerusalem the four pillars of the Church, Peter, James (the brother of the Lord), John, and Paul, to arrange the preaching in the whole world (v. 9). Paul represented the door opened wide for receiving the Gentiles into the faith. So this council, that is, the council of Jerusalem in the year 50 A.D., was the oldest historical document of the early Church, among the apostolic canons, concerning the acceptance of the Gentiles.

2.2.0.en: The wisdom of the Apostle Paul led him to take with him his disciple Titus the Greek, and he openly declared that he was not circumcised. None of the pillars of the Church opposed him; rather, their opinions were united in not obliging the Gentiles to circumcision or the ordinances of the Law. On the contrary, they supported Paul, although he had circumcised Timothy so that the Jews would accept him to preach among them, and not out of a belief that circumcision was necessary.

2.3.0.en: False brethren brought in: that is, Satan brought them in, as tares are sown among the wheat, with the aim of dividing the Church.

2.3.1.en: Privily: in secret, so as to be like moths that eat away the holy building and nullify the liberty which is in Christ.

2.3.2.en: Here Paul explains the reason for his going to Jerusalem and the purpose of his preaching, which is to refute the opinions of the false teachers, who cast doubt on his preaching and hinder the growth of the Church. For these teachers proclaim the necessity of circumcision and the works of the Law, so that they would enslave the Christians of Gentile origin to these symbolic matters and nullify their freedom in life with Christ, which does not need these matters, since the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace, such as prayers and fasts ... etc., have taken their place.

2.4.0.en: We gave place (we yielded): we surrendered.

2.4.1.en: Paul stood against them with courage and showed no compliance or appeasement, and firmly rejected what they proclaim, in order to preserve the right of the Gospel in the freedom that is in Christ by the work of grace: "knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel" (Phil 1:17). We see Paul elsewhere agreeing to the circumcision of Timothy so that he could win the Jews to Christianity, because he was of Jewish origin. Thus the Holy Spirit guides us to act in a way that does not cause the ministry to stumble.

2.4.2.en: The Church believes in the opinion of the council, that is, the council of bishops, to lead the Church, and likewise the council of the priests and servants who guide their church, so that she does not act on a private opinion without returning to those in authority. If you are in authority, take care to obtain the agreement of the other leaders, so that you keep the peace of the ministry and stay away from divisions, because peace within the Church is more important than any project or new idea that disturbs the Church.

2.5.s.en: (2) Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles

2.5.0.en: Those who seemed to be somewhat: they are the pillars of the Church, that is, James, Peter and John.

2.5.1.en: Man's person: that is, looking at a man's position and fame.

2.5.2.en: Paul did not diminish the dignity of those who seemed to be somewhat, but equates his apostleship with theirs: "For in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing" (2 Cor 12:11). That is, all the glory returns to the work of God in the Church: "But by the grace of God I am what I am ... but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Cor 15:10). So there is no difference between one apostle and another, whatever his standing, because the One working in them all is the Holy Spirit. For this reason none of the apostles advised him anything contrary to his preaching, because he had received it by revelation directly from Christ; on the contrary, they approved of his preaching and their opinions agreed together. If Paul defends his apostleship, it is to establish the right faith and not for the sake of his personal honor.

2.6.1.en: The uncircumcision: the absence of circumcision, by which the Gentiles are meant.

2.6.2.en: The circumcision: by which the Jews are meant.

2.6.3.en: Was committed: it appeared from the guidance of the Holy Spirit to Paul and his preaching among the Gentiles that God had entrusted him and directed him to the ministry of the Gentiles.

2.6.4.en: James: he is the brother of the Lord, that is, the son of Alphaeus, one of the disciples of Christ, and he was bishop of Jerusalem; as for James the son of Zebedee, Herod had killed him (Acts 12:2). Cephas: Peter.

2.6.6.en: The apostles, the pillars of the Church, who are Peter, James and John, rejoiced in Paul's zeal and supported him by sending Barnabas with him, "the right hands of fellowship." The right hand of fellowship means a handshake with the right hand, signifying sharing in one ministry, that is, that he might support him in preaching among the Gentiles. Their support was strong, because it came from those who were of reputation among the Jews. This is the spirit of Christian ministry: there is no jealousy among the saints, because the goal is one, which is the salvation of the peoples, and the One working in them is one, who is the Holy Spirit and not the human self. Therefore we find John the Baptist saying of Christ, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Jn 3:30).

2.7.0.en: None of the pillars of the Church advised Paul anything except to help the poor of Jerusalem at the time of the famine, since Herod had begun by killing James the brother of John with the sword, imprisoning Peter, and mistreating the Christians (Acts 12).

2.7.1.en: May we review the goal of our life: do we live for ourselves, or is our goal the glory of Christ and the spread of His Kingdom?! Then we will feel for those around us and try to help them with all our strength.

2.8.0.en: Antioch: Antioch of Syria, which is different from Antioch of Pisidia.

2.8.1.en: I withstood him: I rebuked him.

2.8.2.en: Certain came from James: Christians of Jewish origin from Jerusalem, whose bishop was James the brother of the Lord.

2.8.3.en: Peter went to Antioch after that, and was eating with Paul and with the Christians of Gentile origin, but when Christians of Jewish origin came, Peter withdrew himself out of shame before them, lest he cause them to stumble. So the Apostle Paul stood against him, because this error was not personal, but also brought down others behind him into the sin of hypocrisy. We see here that Paul was courageous, while Peter, and behind him Barnabas and some of the Christians of Jewish origin who were in Antioch, were ashamed to declare that the Christians of Gentile origin are the same as the Christians of Jewish origin, and that they are not required to have circumcision and the Law in order to receive salvation. So they did not eat with the Christians of Gentile origin in front of the Christians of Jewish origin, as if they were declaring the uncleanness of the Christians of Gentile origin, or that they were eating foods that Christianity does not approve, although Christianity has no forbidden foods as Judaism does, which forbade some foods for the sake of spiritual symbols that ended with the appearing of Christianity.

2.9.0.en: They walked not uprightly: that is, they walked in hypocrisy.

2.9.1.en: Paul considered that the conduct of Peter and Barnabas was not according to the uprightness of the Gospel, because by this conduct they regard the Gentiles as sinners. And if Peter, who is of Jewish origin, lives without being bound by the Law, as is proved by his eating with the Gentiles of the foods forbidden to the Jews, why does he compel the Gentiles to live as Jews, that is, to keep the Law?

2.9.2.en: Some of the Fathers, such as St. John Chrysostom and St. Jerome, see that this action of Peter was by arrangement with Paul, to give an opportunity for Paul to rebuke him and for him to be silent, so that the Jews would be assured that compelling the Gentiles to live as Jews is wrong.

2.9.3.en: Do not be afraid to declare the truth, whatever the standing of those who oppose, especially if their conduct causes others to stumble. Ask God's help to give you wisdom in speech, so that you win everyone. And if someone is troubled, you will win him by love after a while, but do not yield the truth for the sake of God.

2.10.s.en: (4) Justification by Christ and not by the works of the Law

2.10.0.en: God forbid: an expression of denial, meaning strong rejection.

2.10.1.en: Paul continues his speech with Peter and says to him: If we, who were born Jews, and not Gentile idolaters, did not benefit from this privilege, since we were not justified by the works of the Law such as circumcision and keeping the Sabbath, but the Law pronounced a sentence of death upon us, then we are sinners like the Gentiles, and therefore we turned to faith in Christ, because Christ is the source of justification and faith in Him is the means of obtaining justification, whereas the works of the Law are not a source of justification. After we have turned to faith in Christ to be justified, do we return to the Law again?! This return would mean that Christ did not justify me, but pushed me to disobey the Law and so caused me to fall into sin, that is, He was a minister of sin, and thereby I place Christ under bondage to the Law "as a minister of sin", that is, the cause of my committing it. God forbid that Christ should be a minister of sin, for the Law was a master over us, taking occasion from sin to pronounce on us the sentence of death as slaves of sin.

2.11.0.en: If I build again the works of the Law, that is, circumcision and living as a Jew, which I had destroyed, I make myself a transgressor, because Christ broke down the wall of partition that was between the Jews and the Gentiles. Thus Paul explained in detail the error into which Peter fell unintentionally, so that all might know the seriousness of its meaning.

2.11.1.en: But St. Peter was not angry; rather, he submitted himself to the rebuke for the sake of the truth of the Gospel, and he said in his second epistle, "Even as our beloved brother Paul" (2 Pet 3:15). Although Peter had supported Paul at the council of Jerusalem in accepting the Gentiles, Paul did not hesitate here to declare the truth and rebuke Peter openly for the salvation of souls. This verse and those after it are either addressed to Peter, or Paul has begun his speech to the Galatians.

2.12.0.en: I through the law am dead: that is, the Law condemned me and carried out the sentence of death on me because I did not keep it. To the law: since I have believed in Christ, I have been freed from the Law and have become dead to it and from it, that is, not bound by it but by the perfect commandments of Christ.

2.12.1.en: Christ died for us and bore our sins in our place, and gave us His life and His freedom that we may live forever, since we were baptized with Him in the likeness of His death and rose with Him, freed from the ritual Law.

2.13.0.en: I am crucified with Christ: Paul feels, as a believer in Christ, that by faith he has been united with the crucified Christ, who fulfilled the Law and paid the debt of sin on the cross by His death. Consequently every believer who is crucified with Christ dies to the Law, and the Law no longer has authority over him.

2.13.1.en: Nevertheless I live: Christ by His resurrection grants me life after the death that had been decreed against me because of sin.

2.13.2.en: Yet not I: not by my own thought and capacities, or my passions and desires.

2.13.3.en: Christ liveth in me: this new life is a gift from Christ, so I live it for Him, and all my thoughts, my words and my actions are for Christ. He is the One who moves me, and He is the One who dwells and works in me, and He is my life. Paul declares, on behalf of every believer in Christ, that his life is founded on faith in Christ, who died out of love for us, so that he lives for Him.

2.14.0.en: Paul makes clear the conclusion of his speech with Peter, or with the Galatians: that the Law does not justify man, otherwise why was there any need for Christ to die? Consequently, clinging to the Law after faith in Christ nullifies this faith and the justification that results from it. Of course Paul did not nullify it, but declares that there is no need to cling to the Law after faith in Christ, whether for Christians of Jewish origin or, all the more, for Christians of Gentile origin, who do not need the Law.

2.14.1.en: May you crucify all evil desires with Christ and die to them so that you may live for Him, and then you will use everything and nothing will enslave you. And as you enjoy the prayers and the readings and are united with Him in the sacrament of Holy Communion, you will feel His presence with you, and even see Him in all the creation around you.

2.14.2.en: Justification by faith and not by the Law
